passages.t: ‘How majestic is Your name’, and the praise of children
passages.happening:
The heading reads, “For the choirmaster. According to Gittith. A Psalm of David” (verse 1).

Psalm 8 is a hymn, a song of praise. It begins and ends with the same line: “O LORD, our Lord, how majestic is Your name in all the earth!” (verse 1). Then: “You have set Your glory above the heavens” (verse 1).

The next line is surprising. God's strength is shown through the weakest people of all: “From the mouths of children and infants You have ordained praise on account of Your adversaries, to silence the enemy and avenger” (verse 2).
passages.hearers:
Gittith is a word no one fully understands. It may name an instrument or a tune. It also heads Psalms 81 and 84.

‘O LORD, our Lord’ uses two different words. The first, in small capitals, is God's personal name. The second means ‘master’ or ‘sovereign’. So the line says: Yahweh, our ruler.

‘Name’ in the Bible means more than a label. It means who someone is, their character and their fame. To say God's name is majestic in all the earth is to say that who God is shines everywhere.

Verse 2 is hard to translate, and Bibles differ. The Hebrew says something like ‘out of the mouths of babies and nursing infants you have founded strength’. The Greek Old Testament put ‘strength’ as ‘praise’, and Matthew quotes it in that form (below). The Berean Standard Bible reads ‘praise’ too. Either way, the picture is the same: God silences his enemies not with armies but through the cries of little children.

In a world that prized strong kings and big armies, this was a reversal. The weakest voices are God's chosen weapon.
passages.later:
When Jesus entered the temple and healed the blind and the lame, children were shouting ‘Hosanna to the Son of David’. The chief priests were angry. Jesus answered them with this psalm: “Have you never read: ‘From the mouths of children and infants You have ordained praise’?” (Matthew 21:16).

Jesus also said that the kingdom of God belongs to those who receive it like little children (Mark 10:14-15). And Paul writes that “God chose the weak things of the world to shame the strong” (1 Corinthians 1:27).

Psalm 19 also sings of what the skies say about God: “The heavens declare the glory of God” (Psalm 19:1). Paul says God's power and nature “have been clearly seen, being understood from His workmanship” (Romans 1:20).
passages.asks:
The psalm begins and ends with God, not with us. Before you think about your own place in the world, it asks you to look up and praise.

And it asks you to listen to the small voices. Children's praise silenced God's enemies. Whose small voice have you been too busy to hear?

passages.t: The night sky, and ‘what is man?’
passages.happening:
The poet looks up at night. “When I behold Your heavens, the work of Your fingers, the moon and the stars, which You have set in place”, he asks: “what is man that You are mindful of him, or the son of man that You care for him?” (verses 3-4).

The answer is astonishing. “You made him a little lower than the angels; You crowned him with glory and honor” (verse 5). “You made him ruler of the works of Your hands; You have placed everything under his feet” (verse 6). Then comes a list: “all sheep and oxen, and even the beasts of the field, the birds of the air and the fish of the sea, all that swim the paths of the seas” (verses 7-8).

The psalm ends where it began: “O LORD, our Lord, how majestic is Your name in all the earth!” (verse 9).
passages.hearers:
With no city lights to hide them, the moon and stars filled the ancient night sky. The poet does not say the sky is a god, as many peoples around Israel did. He calls the moon and stars the work of God's ‘fingers’, as easy for God as delicate handiwork.

‘Man’ in verse 4 means a human being, man or woman. The Hebrew word often suggests weakness and mortality. ‘Son of man’ in the next line is a Hebrew way of saying the same thing again: a human, a child of Adam. Set against the sky, a human being looks tiny.

‘A little lower than the angels’ is how the Berean Standard Bible renders verse 5. The Hebrew word is elohim. Most often elohim means ‘God’. It can also mean ‘gods’ or heavenly beings, such as angels. So Bibles differ here. Some say ‘a little lower than God’. Some say ‘than the heavenly beings’. The Greek Old Testament, made before Jesus' time, read ‘angels’, and the Berean Standard Bible follows it here and notes the other reading. The difference comes from how to translate the word, not from a different text.

‘Crowned with glory and honor’ is royal language. Glory, honour and a crown belong to kings. The psalm gives a king's dignity to every human being. ‘Under his feet’ is a picture of rule; kings were shown with what they ruled beneath their feet.

The list of animals follows the order of creation in Genesis 1: animals of the farm, wild animals, birds, fish.
passages.later:
Genesis 1 says the same thing in prose. God made humankind in his image, male and female, “to rule over the fish of the sea and the birds of the air, over the livestock, and over all the earth itself” (Genesis 1:26). And Genesis 2 shows what that rule looks like: God placed the man in the garden “to cultivate and keep it” (Genesis 2:15).

Job turns the same question into a complaint: “What is man that You should exalt him, that You should set Your heart upon him” (Job 7:17). He means that God watches humans too closely.

The New Testament reads Psalm 8 of Jesus. Hebrews quotes verses 4 to 6, following the Greek: “You made him a little lower than the angels; You crowned him with glory and honor” (Hebrews 2:7). Then it says, “Yet at present we do not see everything subject to him. But we see Jesus, who was made a little lower than the angels, now crowned with glory and honor because He suffered death” (Hebrews 2:8-9).

Paul also uses verse 6 of the risen Christ: “God has put everything under His feet” (1 Corinthians 15:27; see also Ephesians 1:22).
passages.hard:
‘Lower than the angels’, or ‘lower than God’? Both are fair readings of the Hebrew word elohim. Here are the main ways readers take it.

Some read ‘God’: humans are made only a little lower than God himself, which fits Genesis 1, where people are made in God's image. Some read ‘heavenly beings’ or ‘angels’: humans stand just below the beings who serve in God's court. The Greek translators took it that way, and Hebrews follows the Greek. Many readers think both ideas are true: humans are ranked close to the heavenly world, and they bear God's image.

How does Hebrews use it? Hebrews reads the psalm in two steps. The psalm says everything is under humanity's feet. But we do not see that yet. What we do see is Jesus, the true human, who for a little while was made lower than the angels, died, and is now crowned. In him the psalm's picture of humanity comes true.

Two more things. First, ‘ruler of the works of Your hands’ does not mean humans may treat creation as they please. The ruler is a steward under God; the earth remains God's work, and Genesis 2 calls people to ‘keep’ it. This psalm does not settle any modern political argument about how to do that. Second, the psalm does not speak to the age of the earth or how living things came to be. It praises God for what he made and for the place he gave human beings. Christians who differ on those other questions can sing it together.
passages.asks:
Next clear night, go outside and look up. Ask the psalm's question: what am I, that God should think of me? Let both answers sink in: you are small, and you are crowned.

Then ask how you are treating ‘the works of His hands’ that are in your care: animals, land, the people around you. A crown given by God is a trust, not a licence.
